American Beaux-Arts eclectically combines classical, Gothic, Renaissance, and Romanesque elements—unified through composition, not stylistic consistency.</Note>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 1: Axial Composition Recognition**
Questions present floor plans or axial diagrams and ask you to identify Beaux-Arts organizing principles. You trace the primary axis, identify the focal point (grand stair, rotunda, entry), and explain how secondary spaces order around it. You distinguish axial planning from grid planning or organic planning.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 2: Institutional Monumentality**
Questions ask why American Beaux-Arts buildings are so large and ornate. You explain: these buildings (libraries, stations, post offices) embodied democratic ideology. The sclea and ornament said "you, the citizen, deserve grandeur." Beaux-Arts made public institutions visible as civic expression.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 3: Eclecticism and Order**
Questions present buildings combining multiple historical references (Gothic tower, Renaissance palace, Romanesque arch). You explain why this is Beaux-Arts, not confused eclectic pastiche: the unifying principle is symmetry, proportion, and hierarchical ordering. The multiple styles are coordinated through composition.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <Callout>The LEA tests your knowledge of **Beaux-Arts** architecture (École des Beaux-Arts, Paris) and its application to American civic and institutional buildings (1880–1920). Questions focus on architectural principles (symmetry, axiality, classical proportions), key examples (libraries, courthouses, museums), and the relationship between Beaux-Arts training and American institutional design. You must understand why American architects traveled to Paris and how that training shaped American civic identity.</Callout>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Forgetting material and craft. Students focus on plan and elevation while ignoring materials—granite, marble, bronze, terracotta—and the craftsmanship required. Beaux-Arts buildings were expensive because they integrated multiple craftspeople: stonemasons, sculptors, muralists, metalworkers. Material honesty was a principle: granite looks like granite, marble like marble.", "Treating all large civic buildings as Beaux-Arts.
